KEY MESSAGE 1... 
Low pressure will begin to develop in the Mid-Mississippi Valley 
midday today and deepen to the northeast into the Great Lakes by 
late this evening. Ahead of this low, a warm front will lift north 
across the region late tonight into the early overnight hours. The 
majority of the region should remain dry through much of the day as 
showers and thunderstorms will enter Northwestern Ohio by 6-8PM this 
evening and move eastward. The chances of thunderstorms will 
decrease further east as we move into the late overnight hours and 
instability will wane. On the note of instability, temperatures 
through out the day will warm into the low 70s with dewpoints 
climbing into the low 60s by late this evening. This will lead to 
marginal instability, in the for of a few hundred J/kg along and 
behind the warm front. Additionally, a strong low level jet of 40-50 
knots out of the southwest will accompany the warm front as it moves 
north. 0-6km Bulk shear of around 50 knots is also expected with the 
low level jet. With this, there is potential for a few stronger 
thunderstorms to produce wind gusts of 50 MPH or greater. Though 
poor lapse rates across the region will limit how much of the low 
level winds mix down and limiting the overall severe weather threat. 
Currently, SPC has much of North-Central Ohio within a Marginal Risk 
for this time period. Severe weather threat should dissipate later 
into the overnight as precipitation chances decrease as well with 
the departing warm front. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...
The associated cold front from the low pressure system will sweep 
through the region west to east Friday morning into the afternoon. 
Showers and scattered thunderstorms are expected with the front as 
it moves through with widespread accumulation expected. Currently 
expecting around 0.25-.50" of accumulation with higher amounts 
possible within thunderstorms. The low level jet and low pressure 
itself has trended weaker over the past couple of model runs. This 
is leading to wind gusts and winds overall being lower, even with 
the strong CAA behind the front. Winds are still expected to be 15-
20 MPH with gusts over 30 MPH possible. The strongest timeframe for 
winds will be after midnight Friday through early Saturday morning 
when the winds shift to be out of the north with a secondary trough 
moving through. The strongest winds are expected to be along the 
lakeshore, generally from the Islands east through Lake County with 
gusts around 35-40 MPH. Winds will begin to subside Saturday morning 
as high pressure begins to build in from the west. 

With the secondary trough moving through and winds shifting to be 
out of the north, lake effect showers are possible across 
Northeastern Ohio and Northwestern Pennsylvania. An additional 
couple tenth of rain is possible with these linger showers, 
primarily around Cleveland and south through Akron due to the 
connection from Lake Huron with the northerly winds. The lake effect 
showers should linger into Saturday afternoon and begin to dissipate 
as drier air moves in with the upper level ridge. Dry weather is 
expected through the remainder of the weekend into early next
week. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...
Behind the cold front, much colder air will be advected into the 
region with the northwest the north flow Saturday into early Sunday. 
Temperatures Friday night into Saturday morning will drop down into 
the mid to upper 30s with areas near the lakeshore staying in the 
40s. Temperatures have trended a few degrees warmer for the region, 
so there is less confidence in needing frost headlines for Saturday 
morning. Northwestern Pennsylvania will be the coldest location in 
the CWA with temperatures in the mid 30s, but winds being 10-15 MPH 
throughout the night may inhibit frost formation. 

Saturday night into Sunday morning will have more widespread 
temperatures at 36 degrees or lower. High pressure will have built 
in across much of the region at this point with only some lingering 
cloud cover and winds becoming light at less than 5 MPH allowing for 
decent radiational cooling. Trends still have the areas east of the 
I-71 corridor away from the lakeshore with an over 50% chance of 
seeing temperatures below freezing. Frost conditions are likely 
elsewhere with lower probability near the lakeshore given the lake 
is still relatively warm. Temperatures will begin to moderate to 
more seasonal highs and lows starting Sunday as the high pressure 
builds to the east and southwesterly flow moves into the region.
